title: Split a Circular Linked List
statement:
You are given `list`, the head of a circular singly linked list: following `next` from the last node brings you back to the head. Cut it into two separate circular lists and return them as an array `[firstHead, secondHead]`.

- The first circle holds the first `ceil(n / 2)` nodes of `list` (counting from the head), where `n` is the number of nodes.
- The second circle holds the remaining nodes.
- Inside each circle the nodes keep the order they had in `list`, each circle's head is its earliest node, and its last node must point back to that head.

Nodes are `ListNode` objects with `val` and `next`. Each case is written as `[list]`, where `list` gives the values met when walking once around the circle from the head. The answer is shown as two value lists, each read once around a returned circle starting at its head.
constraints: The list has between 2 and 10^5 nodes
The last node's next is the first node
notes:
## Intuition

The simple way is to walk once around the circle, count the nodes, and then walk again to the cut point. Fast and slow pointers find the cut in a single walk: `fast` moves two steps for every one step of `slow`, so when `fast` reaches the end of the circle, `slow` stands on the last node of the first half. The end is detected by a pointer whose next step would land back on the head.

## Approach

1. Start `slow` and `fast` at the head `list`.
2. While neither `fast.next` nor `fast.next.next` is the head, move `slow` one step and `fast` two.
3. If `fast.next.next` is the head, the count is even and `fast` sits one node before the tail, so step `fast` once more. Now `fast` is the tail and `slow` ends the first half.
4. Let `second` be `slow.next`, the first node of the second half.
5. Close the first circle with `slow.next = list` and the second with `fast.next = second`.
6. Return `[list, second]`.

## Example 1, step by step

The circle is `1 -> 5 -> 7 -> 1`. Both pointers start at `1`. Neither `fast.next` (`5`) nor `fast.next.next` (`7`) is the head, so `slow` moves to `5` and `fast` to `7`. Now `fast.next` is the head, so the loop stops; `fast.next.next` is `5`, so `fast` already is the tail. `second` is `7`. Setting `5.next = 1` gives the circle `[1, 5]`, and `7.next = 7` gives `[7]`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n): `fast` covers the circle once.
- Space: O(1): only a few pointers; the nodes are relinked in place.

## Pitfalls

- There is no `null` at the end; compare with the head `list`, or the loop never stops.
- With an even count the loop stops with `fast` one node short of the tail; forgetting the extra step leaves the tail outside the second circle.
- Odd counts put the extra node in the first half (`ceil(n / 2)`), which is where `slow` naturally ends.
- Read `slow.next` into `second` before overwriting it.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `list` | head of the input circle, and head of the first half |
| `slow` | moves one step at a time; ends on the last node of the first half |
| `fast` | moves two steps at a time; ends on the tail of the whole circle |
| `second` | head of the second half |

narration.2: The slow pointer starts at the head.
narration.3: The fast pointer starts at the head too.
narration.4: Keep going while fast can take two more steps without returning to the head.
narration.6: Fast moves two nodes, so slow stays at the middle of what fast has covered.
narration.9: If fast is one node short of the tail, the node count is even.
narration.10: Step fast onto the tail so it can close the second circle.
narration.13: The node after slow starts the second half.
narration.14: Close the first half by pointing its last node back to the head.
narration.15: Close the second half by pointing the tail to its new head.
